newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Envoy says only U.N. can resolve Afghan issue.
newsitem.headline: Envoy says only U.N. can resolve Afghan issue.

text.p: U.N. envoy Norbert Holl launched a fresh ceasefire initiative on Monday, warning that only the world body could offer a long-term solution to Afghanistan's civil war.

In an apparent reference to efforts by Afghan neighbour Pakistan to broker a cease-fire between Taleban-held Kabul and ousted military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, Holl said no single country could resolve the Afghan conflict alone.

"People may think in Kabul it is more important to follow the advice of other negotiators but in the long run help for reconstruction will only come from the international community," he told a news conference in Kabul.

The Taleban, which has been defending Kabul since its September 27 takeover, and Masood both offered on Monday to conditionally accept a ceasefire mediated by Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar.
The Taleban have demanded first an exchange of prisoners while Masood's forces, which hold ground half an hour's drive north of the capital, have called for the demilitarisation of Kabul.

There was no immediate sign on the ground of a ceasefire, which had been due to take effect at midday (0730 GMT). The two sides traded rocket and artillery fire north of Kabul on Monday afternoon, witnesses said.
Holl said he had held talks with Taleban representatives in the capital and was due to fly to the Taleban's southern stronghold of Kandahar on Thursday.
He said he would also be meeting northern leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, who is currently allied with Masood.

While praising Babar's efforts, Holl said he hoped that the Pakistani team would remain in close touch with his people, and made it clear no unilateral initiative was going to end Afghanistan's civil war.
Pakistan is widely regarded as backing the Taleban, although Karachi has denied support of any side.
"In my view no country can solve the Afghanistan issue alone. Afghanistan as you all know needs international support and international solidarity.

"It may look differently to some Afghans now their priorities are different, but in the long run... when it comes to the reconstruction of Afghanistan, there's no doubt in my mind this can be achieved only with international solidarity and certainly not with the help of one country alone," he said.
Holl said that in six meetings with Taleban leaders he had yet to meet its leader Mullah Mohammed Omar, adding it was unlikely any serious progress would be achieved with the Taleban without him.

Separately, Taleban Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told reporters that Kabul was effectively demilitarised, saying no Taleban fighters were in the city, and only what he called a police force remained.

While not referring directly to Masood's recent demands that the city be demilitarised, he said: "In a practical sense Kabul is demilitarised" and Taleban fighters are in their bases outside the city, he said.
